items.followUp: Name the elements of Group II and write their symbols.

rubric.description: Names the elements of Group I.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly listing the elements, including hydrogen.

rubric.description: Writes the symbols of the Group-I elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly matching the symbols to the listed elements.

modelAnswer: Group-I elements are hydrogen (H), lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs) and francium (Fr).

items.followUp: Explain why atomic size generally decreases across a period.

rubric.why: Identifies the increase in nuclear charge across a period.
rubric.description: States the relevant periodic trend in nuclear charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that nuclear charge increases across a period.

rubric.why: Connects the trend to stronger attraction for electrons.
rubric.description: Explains why electron affinity and electronegativity show the same general trend.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons more strongly; accept a clear statement that both properties generally increase across a period.

modelAnswer: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while atomic size generally decreases.
The stronger attraction of the nucleus for electrons increases both electron affinity and electronegativity.

items.followUp: What is a non-polar covalent bond?

rubric.why: Identifies unequal sharing of the bonding electrons.
rubric.description: States how the electron pair is shared in a polar covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the bonded atoms share electrons unequally.

rubric.why: Explains the resulting separation of charge.
rubric.description: Describes the effect of unequal sharing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the electronegativity difference to partial charges on the atoms.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond becomes polar when the bonded atoms have different electronegativities and share the bonding electrons unequally.
The more electronegative atom becomes partially negative (δ−), while the other becomes partially positive (δ+).

items.followUp: Define force and state its SI unit.

rubric.description: Defines pressure as force acting per unit area.

rubric.why: Identifies the SI unit of pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pascal (Pa) or newton per square metre (N/m²).

modelAnswer: Pressure is the force acting normally per unit area of a surface.
Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), equal to one newton per square metre (N/m²).

items.followUp: Why does hydrogen diffuse faster than carbon dioxide?

rubric.why: Compares the molecular masses of hydrogen and oxygen.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen molecules are lighter than oxygen molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that H₂ has a lower molecular mass than O₂.

rubric.why: Links lower molecular mass to faster diffusion.
rubric.description: Explains the difference in diffusion rates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the lighter H₂ molecules diffuse faster (as described by Graham's law).

modelAnswer: H₂ has a much lower molecular mass than O₂.
Therefore, H₂ molecules move and diffuse faster than O₂ molecules (according to Graham's law).

items.followUp: A solution contains 8 g of solute in 40 g of solution. Calculate its mass percent.

rubric.why: Identifies the two masses used in the definition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the mass of solute and total mass of solution.

accept: mass of solute/mass of solution x 100
rubric.description: States the formula for mass percent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio multiplied by 100.

modelAnswer: Mass percent (mass/mass %) is the mass of solute present in 100 parts by mass of solution.
Mass % = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.

items.followUp: Why does a colloidal solution show the Tyndall effect?

rubric.why: Distinguishes the particles in a true solution from larger dispersed particles.
rubric.description: States that true-solution particles are extremely small.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that solution particles are too small to scatter visible light.

rubric.why: Connects the small particle size to the absence of the effect.
rubric.description: Explains why a solution does not show the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles do not scatter a beam of light.

modelAnswer: The particles in a true solution are extremely small.
They do not scatter the beam of light, so a solution does not show the Tyndall effect.

items.followUp: What conditions are necessary for iron to rust?

rubric.why: Identifies the substances involved in rusting.
rubric.description: States that iron reacts in the presence of oxygen and water or moisture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying iron, oxygen and water/moisture.

rubric.why: Identifies the product of the process.
rubric.description: States what forms on the iron during rusting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming rust as hydrated iron(III) oxide, commonly written Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

modelAnswer: During rusting, iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water or moisture.
A reddish-brown layer of hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O), called rust, forms on the iron.
